## 3. Movies for my 15 year old daughter - seeking suggestions from women mainly

**Score:** 98
**Body:** My daughter is getting into movies and I love movies, but I've realised that I have a very stereotypical masculine journey and taste in movies. My favourites as a teen, my exploration of 70s,80s,90s classics as a 20-something film snob and anything I'm into now is a bit too boyish...most my suggestions fall flat, or land in the meh pile for her. She's not into action, fantasy, sci-fi. She likes romance, comedy, drama, non gore horror. I'm looking for interesting female characters, directors, well made movies that help her fall in love with movies more. 

  
Also she has a habit of dual screening while she watches, so avoid any naval gazing stuff.

  
As per title I would prefer female perspective on this or at least other fathers who solved this puzzle.

## 4. films where you can tell the shoot was miserable and it ended up on screen

**Score:** 50
**Body:** Watched The Abyss again last week and the thing that makes it work is that everyone genuinely looks cold and worn out, because apparently they actually were. Ed Harris still wont talk about making it in interviews. Fitzcarraldo is the other obvious one, by the end youre not really watching acting anymore.

Im not after the behind the scenes docs though, i mean the finished film where the misery leaked into it and made it better. Anything else like that?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I think Shelly Duvall had said making The Shining was a nightmare for her and it shows on the screen.
  - I just saw Popeye for the first time, and I couldn’t believe the difference between the two performances.
2. The Island of Dr. Moreau with Marlon Brando
  - I still strangely like this movie but you can absolutely tell what a mess it was. It so fucking weird to start and then the tales of the behind the scene stuff just add to it.
  - I know one of the actors who worked on that. He's one of the biggest pot heads I've ever met, and he said that the amount of pot smoking on that set was too much even for him. 
3. Super Mario Bros. (1993)
  - You should spot the scenes where Hoskins and Leguizamo are drunk.
  - Ha, perfect example. Hoskins got asked years later what the worst job hed ever done was and just said Super Mario Bros, and i think he gave the same answer for biggest disappointment. You can see it on him in the film, he looks knackered in every scene.
4. Titanic was similar 
5. Well I can't say it made it better, but  The Conquer, staring John Wayne was filmed outside of St George, UT on soil that was blown there from the Atom bomb testing site. The had horses and sword fights kicking up the soil to a crazy amount. 45 of the 200 person cast and crew died of cancer. Including John Wayne, Susan Hayward, and Agnes Moorehead. 

It's a famously bad movie to add insult to injury. 

## 5. Lair of the White Worm - Ken Russell - Supernatural Horror comedy [1988]

**Score:** 41
**Body:** Amusing, stylish, sexy and scary, this is a such a fun ride - I haven't seen it getting mentioned so maybe it will be a surprise for somebody.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. absolute fever dream of a movie, in the best possible way
2. Great flick. 
3. Young Hugh Grant gives a spirited performance.   Also, based on a Bram Stoker story.
4. I've loved this film since I was a teenager 
  - Same
5. Saw it in the theater when it opened and stuck with me ever since.
6. Completely off the rails in the best way 
7. I fucking love Ken Russell movies.
8. As a huge Ken Russell fan this is my “intro to Ken Russell” movie. It’s a little more straightforward and than some of his other stuff while still having some major acid trip sequences, and just having Hugh Grant and Peter Capaldi in the leads makes it feel more familiar/comforting to people. Then you hit them with The Devils
9. Not every Ken Russell film is good but there's none not worth watching.

## 1. What are some of your favourite chaotic and messy relationships in movies that actually feels real? I'll go first:

**Score:** 469
**Body:** Joel Barish and Clementine Kruczynski in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004).

I feel that the movie does a really amazing job at showing how these two entirely different people come together and make it work as a couple and even when they slowly drift apart from each other, it feels believable and visceral and makes you connect to their emotions and situations in the film.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Not a movie, but Jimmy and Kim in *Better Call Saul* feel like they're both made for each other and horrible for each other at the same time. It feels super authentic.

## 3. Why are British people so good at playing American characters?

**Score:** 259
**Body:** Why are British actors so good at playing American characters, especially Black American characters? I’ll be watching a movie or TV show and sometimes won’t even realise the actor is British until afterwards, then I’m genuinely caught off guard by how accurate their accent was.

It also makes me wonder why British actors seem to get so many American roles. Is it because their acting schools and training are better, or is there just a particularly strong culture of acting and theatre over there? Obviously there are loads of talented actors in the US, but I’ve always found it interesting how often British actors can completely disappear into American roles, accents and all.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It's probably an essential skill for high level actors. If Hollywood was in England I'm sure more American actors would make more of an effort to have a believable English accent. It's all about employability I imagine. 
  - Even if there wasn’t an American Hollywood, British actors would need to be proficient in accents. The UK has a plethora of regional and local accents. These often inform elements of the character. Being Northern for example was a characteristic in game of thrones and many other shows and movies. 
    - The accent's in game of thrones were largely appallingly bad.  The Starks constantly shifted between Yorkshire and Lancashire accents, which are nothing alike.  John Snows was especially egregious.
  - That’s makes sense 
    - Yeah, it's supply and demand. The UK has a long history of taking the acting profession seriously, with many of the world's best acting schools, a world-leading amateur and youth theatre pipeline, and English as the default language. This creates a supply of talented, skilled, and professional British actors.

The US entertainment industry is a behemoth creating demand in the form of well-paid acting jobs. British actors playing iconic roles in US-made series is where the two sides meet visibly.
  - Most of the famous actors have extensive stage experience in West End as well. They are highly trained and rise through the ranks vs being 'pretty.'
2. Our shared language and exposure to US culture by way of music and movies means we are likely to have absorbed a tonne of American media from a young age.

Our theatre traditions go back some 500 years, I mean some of the buildings we perform plays in are older than the US. We love actors over here.

But it's not universal. Take Jason Statham for example, his American accents are terrible (no shade to JS, I think he's great). It also depends on the coaching they get - if you watch Tom Holland in the first Spider-Man film he did, his accent is all over the place but now it's very good!
3. Britain largely produces actors, America largely produces movie stars. 
4. I’ve seen enough Doctor Who episodes to know that some British actors can do a fantastic job of faking an American accent, and some get handed a paycheck for showing up on time.
5. We have a huge amount of American tv shows and movies that are on out tv. As a kid in the 80s it was all about American shows with badass cars and vehicles for me

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Just want to talk about once of my favourite films ever!

**Score:** 27
**Body:** Perfect Blue (1997) directed by the Japanese director Satoshi Kon, imo is one of the greatest films ever made. It's an 80-something minute long film, and it's actually unbelievable how much it is able to achieve in such a short duration. 

Animation is an absolutely incredible medium for Kon, as he adds so much intentionality and nuance into every scene, that it totally transforms the picture. For example, when Me-mania is first introduced at the concert, and he literally frames Mima in his hands, putting her on a pedestal giving us such an insight into how this person views Mima. Another absolutely incredible way is the way he morphs the faces of Me-mania with Rumi, as well as that of the photographer who kills her image as an icon forever (with the gravure pictures), adding so much to how we look at the story, and whether this could actually be a figment of Mima's imagination. 

The use of colors (aptly as the name is Perfect Blue) is also so fascinating, the use of blues and reds, to really get a read on Mima's mental status as she's falling into a state of supposed psychosis is incredible. This can also be coupled by the use of music, as themes composed by Masahiro Ikumi add so much to these moments and makes it really fascinating trying to piece a version of the story that makes most sense to you. 

The story is incredibly riveting, although it can be very confusing to someone on their first watch, but Kon's ability to weave such a complicated story, yet keep so believable is masterful. The themes explored in the film, dare I say are almost prophetic. The rise of social media, and cyberbullying and the almost parasocial nature it takes on with some people. The idea of mental illness, and how it can be so easy to let go of one's sanity when things are expected of you by people, how one can literally lose parts of themselves, just to fit in and expect to fulfill the role they believe is expected of them. The ideas of social isolation, and how much it can really be detrimental when surrounded by those who don't have your best interests at heart, is something that's so poetically and almost figuratively painted on for the viewer, it's a cinematic masterpiece. 

Another incredible feature of Kon's films is his use of symbols. May it be the fetal position she takes in the bath tub, or the school of fish she feeds and later finds dead, it adds so much to the overall storytelling. Some scenes of her, facing herself as the icon are so beautiful and profound. Also, the final scenes of her running away from Rumi, and the persona shifting between herself and the actual body of Rumi, are some of the greatest in the whole film. It so amazingly shows the internal turbulence that Rumi experiences with Mima rising as a young icon and actress, while she wasn't afforded the same opportunities, as well as that of Mima where she battles her inner self where she believes she is betraying herself (the image of the perfect icon) with these other opportunities, and thus in combat with her own self. Both of the rape scenes, one in the club which is built up to be so realistic and deliberate that one would imagine her really to be danger, to symbolise the death of her idol persona and the supposedly real one perpetuated by Me-Mania, choreographed in such a dramatic and unrealistic way, and finished with her wrapping up the shoot is so delicious and really fascinating to explore. 

Every shot of this film reveals more and more secrets that the director has hidden for his viewers, and it's absolutely my favourite thing on rewatches to experience it wholly again and make up a new hypothesis as to the fate of Mima and what really happened in these 80 minutes. I love that there is no clear explanation to the events that unfolded, and every rewatch adds far more questions than answers, but I believe that's the point of the film. It aims to question and explore, not stifle and constrict. It wants you to experience cinema in its truest form, and really think about beyond the story and into your own minds. I don't know of any other film that does what Perfect Blue has done, especially with the incredibly limited resources Kon had at his disposal in 1997, almost 20 years ago, before the modern age of the internet. It's an experience that I believe everyone should have at least once in their lives, and should definitely be commemorated as one of the greatest films of all time. 

Sorry for the literal essay, but I am just that excited. Lmk what you guys think of the movie and would LOVE to discuss your theories and explanations for the film.

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. When Kon was making films pretty much the only Japanese animator getting any attention was Miyazaki and he was just starting to get that attention in the late 90s early 2000s. Kon's movies were much less kid friendly too and the marketing wasn't there. Then he died tragically young. He'd have much bigger platform today if his films were now being released.
2. You know you're doing something special in animated film when your work influences live action filmmaker's like Aronofsky and Nolan just a few years later. 

Unfortunately even classic animated films do not get mentioned when often when compiling greatest film lists.
  - it's a travesty not to. Arronfsky and Nolan basically copied this artist (I mean there's literal scenes stolen bit by bit) yet fail to recognise and give credit where it's due.

## 2. I recall hearing/reading in the time since its release, that Days of Thunder was a failure. Is that accurate?

**Score:** 20
**Body:** My film snob friends are often in disbelief when I tell them Robert Towne wrote the script.  Yes, *that* Robert Towne. It was nominated for an OSCAR. Against $60M, the film grossed $157,920,733.00 in the box office and that doesn't count one cent of the earnings it made in the last 36 years since on video rental, and later home video, DVD, Blu-ray, TV, and later streaming and VOD purchase.  

But at the time and just after the time, I feel like hearing/reading that the film was considered a dud. Surely it would have been unfair at the time to expect or suggest that it should do parallel business to Top Gun, which was the highest grossing film of 1986, and for a minute, the 11th highest grossing film of all time.  

And yes, I am aware from the sensational and unbelievable [biography of the late Don Simpson](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0747536112?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback) of the countless outrageous delays/arguments/rewrites/extravagances of the set and its producers.

But setting aside critical acclaim, personal opinion, artistic merit, etc., from a performance standpoint, why do some consider the film a stiff?  Was that ever really the case?

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. At the time it was seen as a disappointment, even though it was profitable, but that’s only because Top Gun was so profitable $360 million off of a $15 million budget.

I think it was also a gut check for the studios on the producer led projects in comparison to the director led ones a decade prior like the failure of Heaven’s gate. On set tales of Bruckheimer and Simpson were starting to make waves.

I love the movie and I love Ebert’s review where he attempted to codify the Tom Cruise formula, and it's a pretty good pass -

1. The Cruise character, invariably a young and naïve but naturally talented kid who could be the best, if ever he could tame his rambunctious spirit.
2. The Mentor, an older man who has done it himself and has been there before and knows talent when he sees it, and who has faith in the kid even when the kid screws up because his free spirit has gotten the best of him.
3. The Superior Woman, usually older, taller and more mature than the Cruise character, who functions as a Mentor for his spirit, while the male Mentor supervises his craft.
4. The Craft, which the gifted young man must master.
5. The Arena, in which the young man is tested.
6. The Arcana, consisting of the specialized knowledge and lore that the movie knows all about, and we get to learn.
7. The Trail, a journey to visit the principal places where the masters of the craft test one another.
8. The Proto-Enemy, the bad guy in the opening reels of the movie, who provides the hero with an opponent to practice on. At first the Cruise character and the Proto-Enemy dislike each other, but eventually through a baptism of fire they learn to love one another.
9. The Eventual Enemy, a real bad guy who turns up in the closing reels to provide the hero with a test of his skill, his learning ability, his love, his craft and his knowledge of the Arena and the Arcana.

The archetypal Tom Cruise Movie is "Top Gun," in which the young fighter pilot, a natural, was tutored by a once-great pilot and emotionally nurtured by an older female flight instructor before testing his wings against the hot dogs of his unit, in preparation for a final showdown.
  - I love that and Ebert was he man but the cruise formula is nowhere near that complicated. 

Prime cruise is, “you’re the best \[fill in the blank\] ever…” the best race car driver, the best bartender, the best pool player, the best lawyer ever, the best lawyer ever again, the best high school entrepreneur, the best secret agent close to a dozen times. 
    - It’s pretty verbose, but I imagine Ebert doing his best Don La Fontaine voice whenever I read it.

Early career it was like “I will be the best by the end of this film”, now it’s just “I am the best” but Days 2 will probably be “I am Ann Hathaway and Tom Cruise will make me the best”

Edit: TBF it’ll make for a better sequel if he’s just part of the racing team with her as a veteran racer and ancillary mentor, like a Nemechek
2. At the time it felt like they were trying to recapture the magic of Top Gun but with cars, which many felt it failed to do. It was seen as somewhat of a disappointment critically and at the box office. 
  - This was the exact statement said by countless people at the time. "So it's Top Gun with cars, just not as good?" It was the same formula but Top Gun had the benefit of the Cold War propaganda film boost that helped propel a lot of 80s film.
3. The numbers mislead in this case. Where Top Gun made a big splash in the culture at the time, Days of Thunder basically received a big, mass shrug. 

I distinctly recall there being a DoT billboard around the corner from where I lived, and nothing more. Which is why it was curious to me that they’re doing a remake or sequel or whatever - nobody was bothered in the slightest by it the first time around so why tf are they bringing it back? 
  - As a younger fella, I wouldn't EXACTLY call it a cult classic, but it is a generally well known movie featuring early Tom and Nicole.

I remember growing up we had it on VHS recorded off HBO or something similar. I expect that's how most under 50 types came to know it, and it was popular and well remembered enough that there's some sort of brand recognition.

Ironically I guess they are once again trying to capitalize off the success of Top Gun by doing a legacy sequel.
    - That makes sense, it’s a generational thing. Also, a movie does oftentimes have 2 lives: its original theatrical release vs. its VHS/DVD/streaming afterlife, with the latter being a lot more successful. 
      - I was surprised to find out Hook with Robin Williams isn't considered a universal all time classic. I always thought that was one of his career defining films.

But it got mixed to negative reviews upon release, and while it made money, it's considered a box office disappointment. Even Spielberg says it's one of his least favorite he's made.

I read a post by someone a while back who remembers seeing Hook in theaters at age 12, thinking it sucked, then never even hearing about it again until recently. He was baffled that it was being discussed and thought it had only been "rediscovered" in the last 10 or so years.

But having seen it myself at age 6 in theaters, I'd always loved it. And so did my friends. We all had it on VHS and as we got older on DVD. I still watch it once or twice a year.

But what really blew my mind is how did he avoid seeing it playing constantly on TV for over 30 years?

I feel the same way about a lot of content from the late 90s and after. I was still fairly young, only in middle school in '99, but it felt like that era had lost the magic from my early childhood.

Now I see people in their 20s looking back on things from that era nostalgically, and I realize it wasn't really pop culture that got "worse", like I thought at the time... I was just aging out.
4. I think it was just that you had Tom Cruise coming off Top Gun, reuniting with Tony Scott and a big budget with fast cars and high production, lots of marketing. 

It wasn’t a bomb, but they probably expected more from it. 

It’s been too long for me to say what made it not great other than a predictable plot and compared to the shots they got of the F-14s, stock cars are going to be a step down. So, big exciting tent pole film, but being compared directly to TopGun…just no one could say it did anything better and critics already aren’t going to fawn over those films for the most part. 

## 3. Claude Chabrol is a good discovery - Bridesmaid and Le Ceremonie

**Score:** 20
**Body:** This post completely spoils both movies, if you didn’t watch them and mind spoilers, just don’t read it and see the movies instead. Very refreshing and interesting thrillers, both of them. 

I discovered this director recently when someone recommended **Bridesmaid** as a horror adjacent movie. 

I was instantly pulled in. Superficially, it is framed as a classic thriller. A guy meets a girl at his sister’s wedding, she seems too good to be true but something is a little off, slowly you realize she’s insane, and eventually the guy needs to decide how to deal with it. But this movie is so much more interesting than just that. 

I think what got me so immersed is that it tells you the story through a perspective of an unusually (for fiction) normal and decent character. The protagonist really acts like a sane, normal person, with a normal life, would in that situation. This beautifully demonstrates a big flaw with sanity when encountering someone abnormal. Normal people assume everyone’s more or less like them. 

They don’t really believe someone they interact with could actually do crazy things. 

The way he initially assumes she is lying and making up stories is actually really reasonable. You’re probably more likely to have experience with people who are making shit up for attention or as a “cute little game” than a real psycho. He assumes some kind of implicit understanding between them that she can sometimes get into her fantastic scenarios without really meaning it, and he is wrong. 

This also leads to the ending where the protagonist does probably the sanest thing you would rarely see in a thriller, which is that upon realizing she actually killed a guy he tells the cops. He doesn’t decide to stay with her and join in, or to mercy kill her or anything like that, he just tells the cops after getting over the shock. That is refreshingly realistic. 

There is another very interesting element though, and that is their relationship, and how it’s simultaneously insane but also completely understandable. From the moment he approached her, this girl not only reciprocated his interest but said he was exactly the person she was looking for and acted like they are in some fatalistic romance. But the guy liked her, and as a viewer I realized that although her behavior was obviously not rational, it was also extremely appealing. I mean, you genuinely like and a girl, find her super attractive, you’d like to have a girlfriend, and she gives you so much enthusiasm right back, you’re not going to try to lessen it, it’s practically intoxicating (See: obsession, except in this movie the guy is really blameless.) 

And you can be normal about it, you can understand that the whole soulmate angle is not the reality, but why not accept the narrative since you’re up for where it leads to, presumably a great relationship. 

So I can completely understand why a totally normal person would not see this as a “red flag” although this behavior is exactly what many people today, e.g. people on reddit would consider such a thing. But when you see it play out, it looks like the best thing in the world. 

Of course, it’s a thriller and it was a bad sign, but it was still played out in a way where you completely understand the protagonist in that situation. 

Overall, a thriller that was both psychologically interesting and very realistic and relatable. The angle where being normal makes you not recognize the insane is excellent. There’s no stupidity, no miscommunication, no deceit, just two people who are both pretty honest, but one interprets everything the other says within the assumed frame of normalcy. 

Second movie I watched after that also impressed me, **Le Ceremonie.** It’s a class-based/eat the rich thriller, I guess you can pull parallels with Parasite though this movie is just so much better. 

Throughout the movie, despite the class dimension, I felt absolutely no sympathy for either of the two women. Sophie, the servant who gets hired by a wealthy family, is rude and off-putting from the start. You can say that the family is a bit patronizing or awkward at worst, but they’re overall pretty decent to her. 

I also like how the movie shows the awkwardness of the situation of  having a servant more than it actually tries to criticize the wealthy family. You want to be formal like the father, it comes off as rude. You want to be encouraging but distant like the mom, it seems patronizing. Friendly and as if you’re equals like the daughter, it’s basically insulting. Interacting with someone who serves you is inherently weird and uncomfortable, and there’s no way around it unless you just fully accept your positions. 

They can’t really win because Sophie hates them and acts like she’s a slave (with tons of freedom) rather than an employee who wanted a job and can’t get anything else. They are very lenient if anything, but Sophie is like a spoiled child, furious every time she’s reprimanded, thrilled to break every common sense rule of conduct like it’s the funniest thing ever. 

She loves her new friend, Jeanne, who may be poor but is the most entitled character I’ve seen in years. Total sociopath, she just really doesn’t give a shit, and Sophie is so thrilled by it you’d think Jeanne was liberating a poor slave rather than both of them just vandalizing their surroundings simply because they think they have the right to it. 

I love how the movie didn’t make them redeemable at all, the fact that the family was rich and had better lives, even if totally undeserved, still didn’t in any way make me root for the two psychos. The personalities of these two women were so incredibly grating (very well performed) and obnoxious that the movie even had a horror effect on me, there’s just something about their type that puts me on edge. 

But, while this might be my subjective reaction and not anything intended, after spending the whole movie profoundly hating their characters for their rudeness, erratic behavior, and entitlement, the ending surprised me. 

When the things escalated and they shot the father, which was brilliantly executed since the two never actually discussed any plans or what they intended, and yet implicitly understood when the time came to kill, I stopped hating them.

When they went for the rest of the family, I got a bit of a kick out of it as if I spent the whole movie watching them being oppressed and now finally getting justice. I realized I could get behind people just killing those who have more than them for no other reason, but it annoys the shit out of me when they just behave rude and entitled in small ways. 

The final ending is great too, they get fucked, and I was back to being ok with that since I didn’t really root for them. 

But in that one moment, I suddenly fully understood their hatred towards that family and the pleasure they took in killing them, and for that to happen without in any way making the villains sympathetic or the villains particularly bad is an incredible accomplishment.

## 5. Primetime’s Funhouse Version of Chris Hansen Undermines Its Own Point

**Score:** 9
**Body:** I want to make something clear upfront: I don’t think Chris Hansen is necessarily a good person, and I’m not interested in defending him as some kind of uncomplicated hero. If anything, what makes Hansen interesting to me is the contradiction at the center of his story. I think you can argue that he was doing something fundamentally worthwhile exposing adults who were attempting to meet kids for sex while also questioning *why* he was doing it and what the show eventually became. He may have been doing the right thing for the wrong reasons, and I think that tension is far more interesting than simply deciding that Chris Hansen was secretly a lunatic. And that’s where my problem with *Primetime* starts.

The movie has this incredibly heightened, almost Rob Zombieesque visual language. Everything feels grotesque and theatrical, like some nightmarish carnival attraction or fun house. The colors, performances, camera work, and horror imagery all seem designed to make the world of *To Catch a Predator* feel diseased and surreal. I understand that this is intentional the movie clearly isn't trying to be a straightforward recreation of reality but I’m not convinced it serves the story it’s telling. For me, that style actually gets in the way of the more complicated movie hiding underneath it. I keep thinking about that monologue where Hansen talks about cleansing the world of some ancient evil, or that almost Joker like image of an emaciated Hansen standing in the dressing room. Moments like that don't make me think more deeply about Chris Hansen they make him feel like a character from a psychological horror movie. Eventually, the question stops being, “What happens when justice, ego, journalism, entertainment, and exploitation become impossible to separate?” and starts becoming, “How insane is this guy going to get?”

And I think that's a much less interesting question. Because the real moral contradiction of *To Catch a Predator* is already fascinating without turning Hansen into a monster. The people being confronted on that show weren't innocent victims of Hansen's ambition. They were adults who believed they were communicating sexually with minors and showed up expecting to meet them. That matters. But it also doesn't automatically justify everything Hansen and NBC did in pursuit of exposing them. There are legitimate questions about journalistic ethics, humiliation as entertainment, ratings incentives, law enforcement, due process, and what happens when exposing wrongdoing becomes profitable television. That's the uncomfortable middle ground I wish *Primetime* trusted more.

Hansen doesn't have to be a hero for the audience to acknowledge that exposing those men had value, and he doesn't have to be a psychopath for us to question his motives. Maybe he genuinely believed in what he was doing. Maybe he liked the attention. Maybe he wanted ratings. Maybe he enjoyed being the guy who walked into the room and delivered judgment. Maybe all of those things were true at once. That's what makes him interesting. A person can perform a socially valuable act while being motivated by ego, ambition, fame, self-righteousness, or careerism. Those contradictions don't cancel each other out they complicate each other. And ironically, I think the movie risks falling into the exact same trap that it's criticizing *To Catch a Predator* for.

*To Catch a Predator* took something genuinely horrifying and morally serious and transformed it into compelling television. It created recognizable characters, catchphrases, suspense, confrontations, and eventually a kind of spectacle around something that should never have been entertaining. But *Primetime*, in criticizing that sensationalism, sometimes seems to sensationalize Hansen in almost exactly the same way. Instead of Chris Hansen walking dramatically into a kitchen to confront a predator, now we have Robert Pattinson's Hansen wandering through this expressionistic nightmare, talking about ancient evil and looking like he's slowly transforming into the Joker. The spectacle has changed, but it's still spectacle. That irony is what really bothers me. The movie seems to want us to question what happens when journalism turns real human ugliness into entertainment, while simultaneously turning Chris Hansen and the story of *To Catch a Predator* into its own lurid carnival attraction. 

And that's why I keep coming back to the idea that a grittier, more grounded approach might have worked better for me. Not because realism is automatically superior to stylization, but because restraint could have forced the audience to sit with the contradictions instead of telling us how grotesque everything is supposed to feel. Show me Hansen doing something worthwhile and then show me the ego behind it. Show me someone being taken off the street who genuinely intended to abuse a child, and then make me uncomfortable with the fact that millions of people are watching humiliation as entertainment. Show me Hansen believing that he's protecting people while simultaneously checking the ratings. Let those contradictions coexist without resolving them for me. That's the movie I find more interesting: not “Chris Hansen was actually insane,” and not “Chris Hansen was secretly a hero,” but something much harder to sit with.

What if Chris Hansen was doing something right for reasons that weren't entirely right? What if *To Catch a Predator*genuinely accomplished some good while also becoming exploitative television? What happens when justice and entertainment become so intertwined that even the people involved can no longer tell where one ends and the other begins? To me, *that's* the moral horror of the Chris Hansen story. And it doesn't need the fun house to be disturbing.
